questions.question: It's a busy week at Ridgeback Farm. Which of these jobs suits an AI chat tool?

answers.text: Turning your rough notes into a welcome text for the new relief milker
answers.feedback: Right. You supply the facts and the tool turns them into a clear message, which you then check before sending.

answers.text: Finding out this week's schedule price for prime steers before you book them in
answers.feedback: Chat tools can give an old or overseas price with full confidence. Get current prices from your processor or agent.

answers.text: Telling you how much pasture cover is on the milking platform today
answers.feedback: The tool can't see your paddocks or your farm software. Without your figures it can only guess.

answers.text: Deciding whether a lame cow needs antibiotics or can wait for the vet
answers.feedback: Animal health calls go to your vet. AI can help you write the question down, but it shouldn't make the call.

questions.feedback: AI chat tools are good at turning information you give them into writing. They can't see your farm and can't be relied on for current prices or animal health decisions.

questions.question: Select ALL that apply: You're using an AI tool to help with this month's staff paperwork. Which details should stay out of the chat?

answers.text: Priya's IRD number and bank account number
answers.feedback: Correct. These are staff personal details. The Privacy Act applies when you use AI tools, so keep them out.

answers.text: The reason Sam was off sick last week
answers.feedback: Correct. Health information about a staff member is personal and sensitive. The tool doesn't need it to draft a roster or message.

answers.text: A grazing client's contact details and stock records
answers.feedback: Correct. That's someone else's information, given to you for a specific purpose. Leave it out.

answers.text: The start times for next week's milkings
answers.feedback: Milking start times aren't personal information. They're exactly the kind of fact the tool needs to draft a roster or message.

answers.text: Staff first names and the days each person is rostered on
answers.feedback: First names and rostered days are fine for a roster job. Using first names or roles is how you keep the rest of their details out.

questions.feedback: Give the tool the facts the job needs and nothing more. Staff personal details, bank details and other people's information stay out of the chat.

questions.question: You want a short text to the team about a change to Saturday's afternoon milking. Which prompt gives the tool the clearest job?

answers.text: Write a message to the team about the change to Saturday's afternoon milking. Keep it short, friendly and easy to read on a phone.
answers.feedback: It has a job and a format but no facts. The tool would have to guess what changed, so you'd spend longer fixing the draft.

answers.text: Text the team: Saturday's afternoon milking starts 2.30 pm, not 3 pm. Jack's on with Priya. Under 50 words. Don't add anything else.
answers.feedback: Right. It covers the job, the facts, the format and what to do with gaps, so there's little left for the tool to guess.

answers.text: You're an experienced farm manager. Write a professional message to all staff about the weekend changes.
answers.feedback: Giving the tool a role and a tone doesn't tell it what the change is. It will invent the details to fill the message.

answers.text: Write the team a message about Saturday's milking. Fill in the start time and who's on with whatever seems sensible to you.
answers.feedback: This invites the tool to guess. Whatever seems sensible to it may not match what's actually happening on your farm.

questions.feedback: A clear prompt covers the job, the context, the facts, the format and what to do with gaps. The facts have to come from you.

questions.question: Your notes for a contractor message don't say what time the job starts. What should your prompt tell the tool to do about that?

answers.text: Pick a sensible start time, such as 8 am, so the message sounds organised
answers.feedback: Any time the tool picks is a guess, and the contractor may take it as agreed. Organised-sounding isn't the same as correct.

answers.text: Say the farm office will confirm the start time closer to the day
answers.feedback: That adds a promise nobody has made. If the office doesn't know about it, the contractor ends up waiting on a call that never comes.

answers.text: Leave the time out and ask the contractor what suits them
answers.feedback: Right. Turning the gap into a question keeps the message true to your notes and gets you the missing fact.

answers.text: Work out the most likely time from the rest of the notes
answers.feedback: The rest of the notes don't contain a time, so the tool can only guess. A guess written up as a fact is how a draft goes wrong.

questions.feedback: Tell the tool what to do when your notes run out. Ask, or leave it out, but don't let it fill gaps with guesses.

questions.question: Your note says "Tuesday would suit. Not booked." The AI draft to Dave says "Just confirming you're booked in for 8 am Tuesday." The rest reads well. What do you do?

answers.text: Send it, because Dave will say so if Tuesday at 8 am doesn't suit
answers.feedback: Dave may simply turn up at 8 am for a job he thinks you've confirmed. Don't rely on the other person to catch your mistakes.

answers.text: Keep the booking for Tuesday but delete the 8 am, since Tuesday is in your note
answers.feedback: Tuesday is in your note as a preference, not a booking. Deleting the time still leaves a commitment that was never made.

answers.text: Ask the tool to rewrite it in a friendlier tone, then send the new version
answers.feedback: A friendlier tone doesn't fix the facts. The rewrite will probably keep the booking and the time.

answers.text: Remove the booking and the time, and ask whether Tuesday suits
answers.feedback: Right. Your note only supports a request, so the message should ask rather than confirm.

questions.feedback: A request can quietly become a commitment in an AI draft. Check every date, time and promise against your notes, and fix anything you can't point to.

questions.question: You've asked an AI tool to summarise your 30-page resource consent. The summary looks tidy. What should you do next?

answers.text: Ask the tool to confirm that its summary is accurate and nothing important is missing
answers.feedback: The tool will usually say yes. Its own reassurance isn't a check against the consent.

answers.text: Ask what conditions or dates it left out, then check the summary against the consent
answers.feedback: Right. Summaries can drop things as well as add them, and the consent is the only source that settles it.

answers.text: Paste the summary into a second AI tool and see if it agrees
answers.feedback: A second tool is just another draft. Agreement between two tools isn't evidence from the consent.

answers.text: File the summary and use it in place of the consent from now on
answers.feedback: A missed condition or reporting date can cost you. Keep using the consent itself for anything you rely on.

questions.feedback: For a summary, check what was added and what was left out. The original document is the source; the summary is a draft.

questions.question: Parked in the ute, you dictate a text to the vet clinic: "We've got fifteen heifers to scan on Thursday." What should you do before sending?

answers.text: Send it straight away, because dictation is accurate when you're parked
answers.feedback: Being parked makes it safe, not accurate. Engine and wind noise can still change what the phone hears.

answers.text: Read the transcript, because noise can turn fifteen into fifty
answers.feedback: Right. A quick read catches a changed number before the clinic plans around it.

answers.text: Ask the AI tool to correct any mistakes in the transcript, then send
answers.feedback: The tool doesn't know what you actually said. It could just as easily tidy up the wrong number.

answers.text: Send it, then ring the clinic later if the numbers look wrong
answers.feedback: By then the clinic may have booked the wrong amount of time. Reading it first takes seconds.

questions.feedback: Voice input is handy, but the transcript is a draft too. Pull over and read it before it goes anywhere.

questions.question: Select ALL that apply: An AI tool has written up the team meeting actions from your notes. Which details do you check against the notes before sending?

answers.text: Days and times
answers.feedback: Correct. Tools often add a time of day or a deadline that sounds normal but wasn't agreed.

answers.text: People's names
answers.feedback: Correct. A name that isn't in your notes means someone is being given a job they never heard about.

answers.text: Numbers, such as paddock numbers or head counts
answers.feedback: Correct. A wrong paddock number or head count sends someone to the wrong place or the wrong mob.

answers.text: Anything that says a job will be done, or has been done
answers.feedback: Correct. Promises and "done" claims turn plans into commitments. Check each one against what was actually said.

answers.text: Only the lines that read differently from how you'd write them
answers.feedback: Made-up details often read perfectly naturally. You have to check the facts, not just the lines that look odd.

answers.text: Nothing, if your prompt told it not to add anything
answers.feedback: A clear prompt cuts down on guesses but doesn't stop them. You still check every fact before sending.

questions.feedback: Check every date, name, number and promise against your notes. A good prompt reduces mistakes, and the check catches the rest.
